incite

in-SITE / rhymes with delight · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To incite someone is to stir them up or push them into a strong reaction or action.

The fiery speech incited the crowd to march on city hall.

Example

The fiery speech incited the crowd to march on city hall, with thousands of people surging forward in unified action toward the government building.

Incite perfectly captures stirring people up and pushing them into specific action. The speaker didn't just trigger anger (provoke); they actively pushed the crowd to march. Incite emphasizes this aggressive push toward action, not just emotional reaction.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

agitate: To agitate is to stir people up and keep them stirred - speeches, pamphlets, and pressure that build unrest over weeks or months. Incite is the final shove: it pushes people over the line into a specific act, right now. Agitators warm a crowd; inciters launch it.

arouse: To arouse is to awaken strong feeling - anger, curiosity, sympathy - and it stops at the feeling. Incite goes one step further and darker: it pushes people past feeling into action, often reckless action. A film can arouse outrage; it takes someone to incite the march.

rouse: To rouse someone is to stir them from stillness into motion, and the word stays neutral about what follows - a coach can rouse a sluggish team at halftime. Incite is charged: it means deliberately pushing people toward strong, usually aggressive action, the way a ringleader whips up a mob.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dissuade: to talk someone out of taking action

deter: to discourage someone through doubt or fear

Where it sits · how strong a reaction gets sparked — encourage → incite → inflame → enrage

encourage vs. incite: Encourage is much weaker than incite: encouraging gently supports someone's action, while inciting pushes people hard toward dramatic, often reckless action.

inflame vs. incite: Inflame is stronger than incite — to incite a crowd stirs it to act, but to inflame it sets emotions blazing past the point of reason.

enrage vs. incite: Enrage is the strongest of the set: incite pushes people toward action, but enrage drives them all the way into furious, uncontrolled anger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: into, upon (Latin)

Root — cit (from citāre)

Root — cit (from citāre): to set in motion, to rouse (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('into') plus citāre ('to set in motion') makes incite literally 'to put into rapid motion' — to stir people up and push them into strong action.

Use the root in a new word: excite

Use the root in a new word: excite: The announcement of a surprise field trip never fails to excite the sixth graders.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / serious

Use incite when you want to show someone stirring people up and pushing them toward significant action (usually aggressive or dangerous). For encouraging something positive, use encourage. For awakening emotion without action, use arouse.
